It contains no\nwarrior code. The language itself is documented in `redcode/`, `guide.htm` and\n`icws94-standard.txt`.\n\n## Archetypes\n\n- **Imp.** `MOV 0, 1` copies itself one cell ahead forever.\n  - Imps are very hard to kill and kill almost nothing, so on their own they mostly tie.\n  - Several imps spaced CORESIZE/n apart and executed in turn form an *imp ring* or\n    *imp spiral*, which is sturdier.\n- **Stone (bomber).** A small loop that drops bombs (DAT to kill, SPL to slow) at a\n  fixed step through the core.\n  - It is small, fast and hard to find.\n  - The choice of step matters: it decides how evenly and how fast the core gets\n    covered.\n- **Paper (replicator).** Copies itself to new places, again and again, and spawns many\n  processes.\n  - Killing one copy does not kill the warrior, so DAT bombs alone rarely beat it.\n  - \"Silk\" papers copy with `SPL`/`MOV` pairs and post-increment pointers.\n- **Scanner.** Looks for non-empty cells (`SEQ`/`SNE`/`JMZ`), then attacks what it\n  found.\n  - Typical attacks: a few bombs, a carpet of `SPL 0` bombs that stuns the target, or a\n    switch into a core clear.\n  - A scanner has to avoid detecting itself, and its speed is measured in cells per\n    cycle (0.5c, 0.66c, ...).\n- **Core clear.** Overwrites the whole core in sequence, typically with SPL first\n  (stun), then DAT (kill).\n  - Clears are used to finish off stunned opponents. The base system includes  a\n16:        graphical  core  display  for  UNIX  (curses,  X-windows)  and PC/linux\n17:        (svgalib). A line-oriented debugger is included to help in writing war-\n18:        riors for the ICWS'94 draft standard.\n19: \n20:        pMARS runs one or more warriors written in Redcode that are provided as\n21:        file(s) on the command line.  Running a single warrior is supported for\n22:        debugging.  Two  warriors  are  pitted  against each other for standard\n23:        play, but up to 36 warriors can be named for \"multi-warrior\" core  war.\n24:        If  the warrior(s) assemble without error they are loaded into the core\n25:        array and executed in round-robin mode starting with the first warrior.\n26:        Warrior 1 is loaded starting at core position 0, warrior 2, 3, etc., at\n27:        either a random or fixed position.  For fairness the starting order  is\n28:        rotated after each round.\n29: \n30: SCORE\n31:        The  score  is reported after all rounds have been played. A round ends\n32:        when either a single surviving warrior remains or when a maximum number\n33:        of  cycles  has  elapsed.   For  each round, every surviving warrior is\n34:        awarded points calculated from a score formula (F).  By  default,  this\n35:        is  (W*W-1)/S, where W is the total number of warriors participating, S\n36:        is the number of of survivors, and \"/\" is integer division. Alternative\n37:        score formulas can be specified with the = option (see below).\n38: \n39:        When two warriors battle, the results are reported as wins1, wins2, and\n40:        ties, where wins1 and wins2 are the numbers of rounds that each warrior\n41:        won,  and  ties  are the number of rounds in which both warriors lasted\n42:        until time-out.  The score is then:\n43: \n44:                warrior 1:  points = wins1 * F + ties * F\n45:                warrior 2:  points = wins2 * F + ties * F\n46: \n47:        F is a score formula containing the W and S parameters.  When more than\n48:        two  warriors  (W)  participate  in  a  game,  results  are reported as\n49:        wins[1], wins[2], .., wins[W], losses for each warrior, where the index\n50:        indicates the number of warriors that survived until the end (S parame-\n51:        ter in the score formula). The total number of points for each  warrior\n52:        is then calculated as:\n53: \n54:                points =  sum (S=1..W) (wins[S] * F)\n55: \n56:        A few alternative score formulas:\n57:                10\n58:                (W+1)/S\n59:                (x=W-S+1)*(x+1)/2\n60:                (S==3)*5 + (S==2)*3 + (S==1)\n61:                (S == 1)*W + (S != 1)\n62: \n63: OPTIONS\n64:        Command  line  options  may occur anywhere on the command line. Single-\n65:        letter options without a parameter can be combined as in -fbe. The spe-\n66:        cial  argument  -  (dash)  stands for standard input (stdin). It can be\n67:        combined with the -@ option (see below) to signify reading options from\n68:        stdin,  or  the  -  can take the place of a  warrior filename, in which\n69:        case warrior code starting with a ;redcode line and ending with an  END\n70:        statement  is extracted from stdin. The END statement can be omitted if\n71:        the next ;redcode line immediately follows the last  instruction.  Sev-\n72:        eral  warriors,  each  specified by a separate dash on the command line\n73:        and bracketed by ;redcode/END can be piped into pMARS.  #- (where #  is\n74:        a  positive number) is a shorthand for writing this number of dashes on\n75:        the command line.\n76: \n77:        -r #   This options sets the number of rounds to play. The  default  is\n78:               1.  -r  0 produces assembly output (unless -b is specified), but\n79:               does not execute the warrior(s). A maximum of 32767  rounds  can\n80:               be specified.\n81: \n82:        -s #   The  -s  option  specifies  the size of core memory in number of\n83:               instructions.  It defaults to 8000. Maximum core size  is  plat-\n84:               form-dependent, but usually at least 65535.\n85: \n86:        -c #   -c  sets  the  maximum number of cycles per round.  A cycle con-\n87:               sists of one execution of each warrior. A round ends when either\n88:               a single warrior remains executing or when the maximum number of\n89:               cycles has elapsed.\n90: \n91:        -p #   This option sets the maximum number of processes a  warrior  can\n92:               run.  The default is 8000.\n93: \n94:        -l #   This  sets  the  maximum  length  of  a  warrior  source file in\n95:               instructions.  It defaults to 100.\n96: \n97:        -d #   This option specifies the minimum  distance  between  the  first\n98:               instruction of each warrior. It cannot be smaller than the maxi-\n99:               mum length (-l option) and defaults to 100 instructions.\n100: \n101:        -S #   The -S option sets the size of  the  P-space  to  #  cells.  The\n102:               default  is 1/16th of core size if core size is evenly divisible\n103:               by sixteen, or the next larger divisible fraction. See also  the\n104:               P-SPACE section below.\n105: \n106:        -R #   The -R option sets the read limit. The read limit must be a fac-\n107:               tor of core size.  The default is core size, i.e. no read limit.\n108: \n109:        -W #   The -W option sets the write limit. The write limit  must  be  a\n110:               factor  of  core  size.  The default is core size, i.e. no write\n111:               limit.\n112: \n113:        -f     The -f option instructs the loader to  use  a  fixed  series  of\n114:               addresses for positioning warriors. This is done by initializing\n115:               the pseudo random number generator with a checksum value derived\n116:               from  the source of all warriors.  Thus, initial placements will\n117:               still be \"random\" from round to round, but will be the  same  if\n118:               the same warriors are run again. As a consequence, the result of\n119:               battles run with the -f option will show no statistical fluctua-\n120:               tions.  This  options is useful for validating ports of pMARS to\n121:               new platforms and for providing an  absolute,  albeit  arbitrary\n122:               performance measure for warriors.\n123: \n124:        -F #   This  option  server two purposes. It sets the seed value of the\n125:               pseudo random number generator, and also  tells  the  loader  to\n126:               install  warrior  2  at  the given address # for round 1. If the\n127:               number is larger than the core size minus  the  minimum  warrior\n128:               distance,  it  will  be wrapped around to the range of available\n129:               starting positions.  This option is useful for testing different\n130:               versions  of a warrior with constant initial placement.  Warrior\n131:               1 is always installed at address 0.  The -F and -f  options  are\n132:               mutually  exclusive.  If neither option is specified, the pseudo\n133:               random number generator is initialized with the system time.\n134: \n135:        -P     This option makes pMARS use an alternative algorithm  for  posi-\n136:               tioning  warriors. This algorithm uses all possible combinations\n137:               of starting order and position in a random  sequence,  and  will\n138:               not  use  the same combination twice unless all the combinations\n139:               have already been used. If the -r option is not given, the  num-\n140:               ber of rounds fought will be the number of all possible combina-\n141:               tions.  Trying to use this option with more (or less)  than  two\n142:               warriors causes an error.\n143: \n144:        -e     If this option is specified, the cdb debugger is entered immedi-\n145:               ately after loading warriors into core.\n146: \n147:        -b     This options runs pMARS in brief output mode. -b suppresses war-\n148:               rior listings after assembly.\n149: \n150:        -A     The  -A  option assembles the input warriors without running any\n151:               fights.  Emits ICWS'94 draft compliant load files.\n152: \n153:        -k     With the -k option, pMARS uses the same  output  format  as  the\n154:               KotH  program. Since  ICWS'94  is  a\n160:               superset  of  ICWS'88,  this  options  is  not  necessary to run\n161:               ICWS'88 warriors.\n162: \n163:        -o     When this option is given, pMARS reports  scores  in  decreasing\n164:               order  rather  than in the order warriors were named on the com-\n165:               mand line. This is\n168:               only useful for debugging.\n169: \n170:        -v     This  option sets the display mode for UNIX and DOS display ver-\n171:               sions (see APPENDIX).\n172: \n173:        -@ <fn>\n174:               pMARS continues reading options and filenames from the parameter\n175:               file <fn>.  If <fn> is a - (dash) standard input is parsed. Com-\n176:               ments in the parameter file start with a semicolon.\n177: \n178:        -= <string>\n179:               The = (equal) option allows you to specify a custom  score  for-\n180:               mula  (see  SCORE).  The formula may contain the standard arith-\n181:               metic and logical operators (as in the C language), as  well  as\n182:               the  parameters W (number of warriors participating) and S (num-\n183:               ber of warriors surviving this round). You need to  enclose  the\n184:               formula  string  with quotes if it contains spaces or characters\n185:               interpreted by the operating system.\n186: \n187:        -Q #   The \"query\" option is intended for use in scripts that run pMARS\n188:               in  batch  mode.  Depending on the number code following -Q, the\n189:               program returns  an  informative  number  as  the  exit  status.\n190:               \"pmars  -Q  1000\" e.g. will cause pMARS to exit with a code that\n191:               spells out the program version. More on -Q  arguments  and  exit\n192:               codes can be found in the ADDENDUM.\n193: \n194:        $      The $ (dollar) parameter is not preceded by a dash and cannot be\n195:               grouped with other options. It terminates reading  command  line\n196:               parameters  and  is used in parameter files or input streams (-@\n197:               fn).  The $ is necessary if you want to combine two or  more  of\n198:               command  line  parameters,  warrior code and cdb commands in the\n199:               same input stream or file. Below an example of such  a  combined\n200:               input file:\n201:                   ;Below the command line parameters:\n202:                   -r 10 -beF 1000 2- $\n203:                   ;redcode\n204:                   ;name Imp 1\n205:                   ;assert 1\n206:                   mov 0,1\n207:                   end\n208:                   ;redcode\n209:                   ;name Imp 2\n210:                   ;assert 1\n211:                   mov 0,2\n212:                   mov 0,2\n213:                   end\n214:                   !! cdb commands follow:\n215:                   sk 1000\n216:                   reg\n217:                   quit\n218: \n219: X-WINDOWS OPTIONS\n220:        The  X-Windows  display  version  of pMARS has these additional command\n221:        line options:\n222: \n223:        -display <string>\n224:               Expects a string specifying the display where the window  should\n225:               appear.  Following X standards, this display specification has a\n226:               format of hostname.domain:display.screen where the  part  before\n227:               the  colon  is the standard internet host specification and dis-\n228:               play and screen are integers.  The screen specification  can  be\n229:               omitted. For an example, consider you are working at an X termi-\n230:               nal named ncd13.complang.tuwien.ac.at and remotely logged in  at\n231:               host  stud1.tuwien.ac.at where the binary of pmars lies, you can\n232:               use the following command line\n233: \n234:          stud1$ pmars -display ncd13.complang.tuwien.ac.at:0 -b aeka.red aeka.red\n235:          and the window will appear at you local screen.\n236: \n237:        -geometry <string>\n238:               Lets you specify the initial size and position  of  the  window.\n239:               The  format  is  widthxheight+x+y  where width, height, x, y are\n240:               integers and + may be replaced by -. Either  of  the  two  parts\n241:               (widthxheight  or  +x+y)  may  be omitted. This overrides the -v\n242:               switch concerning the window  geometry.  As  an  example,  pmars\n243:               -geometry  600x400+30+100 ....  will open a window of 600 by 400\n244:               pixels  at  the  screen  position  (30,100).   pmars   -geometry\n245:               1024x768  ...  creates  a  window  of  1024x768 pixels and pmars\n246:               -geometry -20+300 ... creates a window with standard  size  with\n247:               its  left  upper  corner  at position (-20,300), i.e. out of the\n248:               left side of the screen.\n249: \n250:        -fn <string>\n251:               The string following this argument specifies the X font to  use.\n252:               By  default,  a  terminal  font  is  used. If this font can't be\n253:               found, \"fixed\" is used for a font (\"fixed\" should be present  at\n254:               every  X  installation).   Use  the  command 'xlsfonts' to get a\n255:               listing of fonts that can be used at your X  server.  'xfontsel'\n256:               provides  a  comfortable  way  to  select a font. \"fixed\" is the\n257:               fallback if the specified font can't be found.  It  is  strongly\n258:               recommended to use a fixed pitch font.\n259: \n260:        The argument of the -v display option has an additional fourth digit in\n261:        the X-Windows version: 0 (the default) enables the color display, 1 the\n262:        grayscale,  and  2  the  black  and white display (e.g. -v 1033 for the\n263:        grayscale display).\n264: \n265: REDCODE\n266:        pMARS implements an extension of the proposed ICWS'94 standard. The new\n267:        instruction  modifiers .A,.B,.AB,.F,.X, and .I, the arithmetic instruc-\n268:        tions MUL, DIV and MOD, as well as post-increment indirect (>) are sup-\n269:        ported.\n270: \n271:        Version  0.5  of pMARS adds support for three experimental opcodes that\n272:        are currently not included in the ICWS'94 draft:\n273: \n274:        SEQ (Skip if EQual): this is a synonym for CMP and is  included  mainly\n275:        for  clarity  (future  versions of pMARS may implement SEQ as a \"prede-\n276:        fined EQU\" rather than a true opcode).\n277: \n278:        SNE (Skip if Not Equal): the opposite of SEQ.\n279: \n280:        NOP (No OPerations): do nothing.\n281: \n282:        Version 0.6 adds three new indirect addressing modes that  use  the  A-\n283:        field instead of the B-field as the pointer for indirection:\n284: \n285:        * - indirect using A-field\n286: \n287:        { - predrecement indirect using A-field\n288: \n289:        } - postincrement indirect using A-field\n290: \n291:        The  new  P-space instructions of version 0.8 are discussed under sepa-\n292:        rate heading below.\n293: \n294:        The assembler also supports multi-line EQU statements,  a  feature  not\n295:        included  in  the  current  ICWS'94  draft.   The format for multi-line\n296:        EQUates is\n297:            <label> EQU <line1>\n298:                    EQU <line2>\n299:                    [...]\n300:                    EQU <lineN>\n301:        <label> in the warrior source is replaced by <line1> <newline>  <line2>\n302:        <newline>  [....]  lineN.  In  contrast  to KotH, pmars EQUs substitute\n303:        arbitrary text, and not just  expressions.   EQU  expressions  are  not\n304:        implicitly parenthesized.\n305: \n306:        pMARS  features the non-standard FOR text-repetition macro.  This macro\n307:        repeats the text between FOR and ROF a specified number of times:\n308:        <labels> <counter> FOR <times>\n309:                           [..]\n310:                           ROF\n311:        <times> is an expression specifying the number of  expansions;  it  may\n312:        contain EQUates and labels as long as they have been defined before the\n313:        FOR/ROF block.  <counter> is the last label before the  FOR  word,  but\n314:        not  necessarily  on  the  same  line.   It  is expanded to 01, 02, ..,\n315:        <times> in each repetition.  The  optional  <labels>  label  the  first\n316:        instruction after FOR expansion. An example:\n317:                ORG start\n318:        start\n319:        sp      FOR 2\n320:        a&sp        SPL a&sp\n321:                    JMP a&sp\n322:                ROF\n323: \n324:        becomes after expansion\n325: \n326:        start\n327:        a01     SPL a01\n328:                JMP a01\n329:        a02     SPL a02\n330:                JMP a02\n331:        The  symbol  &  concatenates 'a' and 01, 02 to form a valid label.  EQU\n332:        expansion and FOR/ROF processing is done  in  the  same  pass.   It  is\n333:        therefore possible to write\n334:        dest01  EQU 500\n335:        dest02  EQU 1000\n336:        dest03  EQU 1500\n337: \n338:        idx     FOR 3\n339:                    MOV src,dest&idx\n340:                    MOV src+1,dest&idx\n341:                ROF\n342: \n343:        src     MOV <-1,<-1\n344:                JMP src,<-2\n345:        Using  predefined EQUates (see below) it is possible to define adaptive\n346:        FOR/ROF blocks. The next example fills the remainder of the warrior (up\n347:        to MAXLENGTH lines) with decoy instructions:\n348:            FOR MAXLENGTH-CURLINE\n349:                DAT 1,1\n350:            ROF\n351:        Since  true  logical  expressions have a value of \"1\" and false expres-\n352:        sions a value of  \"0\",  you  can  write  conditionally  assembled  code\n353:        enclosed by FOR/ROF:\n354:            FOR CORESIZE == 8000\n355:            <some code>\n356:            ROF\n357: \n358:            FOR CORESIZE != 8000\n359:            <other code>\n360:            ROF\n361:        pMARS  uses KotH-style ;name and ;author comments to describe warriors.\n362:        If a line starting with ;redcode is present, all text preceding  it  is\n363:        ignored. This makes it possible to run posted warriors without removing\n364:        mail headers and descriptive text.  The ;version, ;strategy  and  other\n365:        comments mentioned in the ICWS'94 draft are currently not used.\n366: \n367:        As  another \"non-standard\" extension, the assembler predefines the fol-\n368:        lowing   run-time   variables:   CORESIZE,   MAXPROCESSES,   MAXCYCLES,\n369:        MAXLENGTH,  MINDISTANCE,  PSPACESIZE, READLIMIT, ROUNDS and WRITELIMIT.\n370:        They can be used in your Redcode as though they were  defined  by  EQUs\n371:        like\n372:            CORESIZE     EQU 55440  ;current value of -s parameter\n373:            MAXPROCESSES EQU 10000  ;current value of -p parameter\n374:            [etc.]\n375:        The run-time variable CURLINE holds the current instruction number off-\n376:        set from the first instruction. WARRIORS is initialized with the number\n377:        of warriors specified on the command line.\n378: \n379:        pMARS  supports  the  ;assert  directive as a way of checking whether a\n380:        warrior is run under the parameters it was designed for. If the expres-\n381:        sion  following  ;assert  evaluates to \"0\" (false), assembly is aborted\n382:        with an error message. If an ;assert is missing, a warning  is  issued.\n383:        Examples:\n384:            ;assert CORESIZE == 55440 && MAXLENGTH >= 200\n385:            ;assert !(CORESIZE % 4)  ; is multiple of 4\n386:            ;assert 1 ; if warrior works under all settings\n387:        The  run-time  variable  VERSION  holds the current pMARS version (e.g.\n388:        \"60\" is v0.6.0) and is useful in ;assert expressions.\n389: \n390:        With the -8 option, pMARS is fully ICWS'88 compatible,  except  that  a\n391:        comma  is  required  between  operands.  Extensions like predefined and\n392:        multi-line EQUs and FOR/ROF are supported even in ICWS'88 mode.\n393: \n394:        A full treatment of corewar and ICWS'94 in  particular  is  beyond  the\n395:        scope  of  this  document. General information about corewar as well as\n396:        the ICWS'94 draft is available  by  anonymous  FTP  from  https://core-\n397:        war.co.uk/standards/\n398: \n399: P-SPACE\n400:        Originating  from  discussions  on  rec.games.corewar,  P-space  is  an\n401:        attempt at making warriors more \"intelligent\" by giving them a  memory.\n402:        P-space,  short  for \"private\", \"permanent\" or \"priviledged\" space is a\n403:        memory area separate from core whose contents is  not  cleared  between\n404:        rounds.  Every  warrior  has  its own P-space for gathering information\n405:        about the opposing warrior, but there is a  provision  for  sharing  P-\n406:        space in team play (see below).\n407: \n408:        P-space  cells contain values in the range 0..CORESIZE-1. The number of\n409:        P-space cells can be adjusted with  the  -S  command  line  option;  by\n410:        default,  P-space  size is 1/16th of CORESIZE. This number is available\n411:        to warriors as the predefined variable PSPACESIZE.   pMARS  updates  P-\n412:        space cell 0 at the beginning of each round with the result of the pre-\n413:        vious round: 0 signifies a loss in the previous round, a number  larger\n414:        than  zero  means that the warrior survived until the end of the round,\n415:        the value indicating the number of surviving warriors. That is, a value\n416:        of \"1\" means that the warrior survived by itself (a \"win\" in a two-war-\n417:        rior battle), a value of \"2\" that two warriors lasted until the end  (a\n418:        \"tie\"  in a two warrior battle), etc..  In the first round, P-cell 0 is\n419:        set to -1 (actually CORESIZE-1) to indicate that there is  no  previous\n420:        result.\n421: \n422:        There are two new instructions for accessing P-space:\n423: \n424:        LDP    (Load P-space) loads P-space cell specified by A-value into core\n425:               at B-address.\n426: \n427:        STP    (Store P-space) stores A-value into P-space cell specified by B-\n428:               value.\n429: \n430:        It is important to note that P-space cells are refered to by A/B-values\n431:        as opposed to A/B-addresses. As an example, \"STP #9,#1\" stores number 9\n432:        in P-cell 1.\n433: \n434:        Since  all  P-space access is only via these two instructions, it takes\n435:        too much time and space to use P-space for working variables where they\n436:        would  be safe from the opposing warrior. P-space was made deliberately\n437:        hard to access, unlike a set of general purpose registers.\n438: \n439:        P-space can also be used for communication between  warriors  belonging\n440:        to  a  team  in multi-warrior core war. To allow communication, P-space\n441:        has to be declared as \"shared\".  You  do  this  by  including  the  PIN\n442:        pseudo-opcode in your source:\n443: \n444:        PIN    (P-space Identification Number) has a single numerical argument.\n445:               If two or more participating warriors have the  same  PIN  argu-\n446:               ment,  they  share the same P-space. If the PIN pseudo-opcode is\n447:               missing from a warrior's source, its P-space  is  strictly  pri-\n448:               vate.  The  PIN  argument  is  not normalized to [0..CORESIZE-1]\n449:               before comparison. \"PIN 0\" and \"PIN CORESIZE\" are therefore  not\n450:               the same.\n451: \n452:        P-cell  #0 holding the result of the last round is exempt from sharing,\n453:        i.e.  every warrior has its own last round cell even though the rest of\n454:        its P-space may be shared.\n455: \n456: CDB DEBUGGER\n457:        Cdb is a line-oriented debugger. It is invoked either by specifying the\n458:        -e option (enter cdb immediately), by including debugging  commands  in\n459:        the  warrior  source,  or by hitting Ctrl-C during the simulation.  The\n460:        debugger is also entered whenever a warrior terminates  (\"post-mortem\")\n461:        if execution was started with the go command.  cdb is very powerful and\n462:        has an overwhelming number of commands. You may want to start with only\n463:        the most often used commands: step (single step execution), go (execute\n464:        until breakpoint), list (look at core),  trace  and  untrace  (set  and\n465:        remove breakpoints), and go on to more complex ones later.\n466: \n467:        The following commands are available at the cdb prompt; commands can be\n468:        abbreviated to the first unambiguous substring.\n469: \n470:        <Enter>\n471:               repeats the last command issued at the cdb prompt.\n472: \n473:        help   displays a brief command summary.\n474: \n475:        progress\n476:               displays the status of the current game in progress.\n477: \n478:        registers\n479:               displays the current state of the simulator,  including  program\n480:               counters and task queues.\n481: \n482:        go     runs  the  simulator until an instruction whose trace bit is set\n483:               is executed. If there are no traced instructions go  returns  to\n484:               the post-mortem debugger.\n485: \n486:        step   executes  the  next instruction in the task queue and returns to\n487:               the cdb prompt.\n488: \n489:        continue\n490:               returns to the simulator to complete the game without  interrup-\n491:               tions.\n492: \n493:        thread is  similar  to step except that only the current task thread is\n494:               traced.\n495: \n496:        skip [count]\n497:               executes the next [count] instructions  in  the  queue  silently\n498:               before returning to the cdb prompt.\n499: \n500:        execute [address]\n501:               resets  the  task  queue of the current warrior to [address] and\n502:               executes it. This is useful in conjunction with edit.\n503: \n504:        quit   aborts pMARS and returns to the OS prompt.\n505: \n506:        trace [range]\n507:               sets the trace bit of the specified address or address range.\n508: \n509:        untrace [range]\n510:               clears the trace bit of the specified address or address range.\n511: \n512:        moveable on|off\n513:               specifies whether the trace bit is copied by the MOV.I  instruc-\n514:               tion. The default is on.\n515: \n516:        list [range]\n517:               displays  the specified range of core addresses, a set trace bit\n518:               is indicated by 'T'.  Unmodified addresses (DAT.F 0,0) are shown\n519:               as blank.\n520: \n521:        edit [range]\n522:               allows  modifying  core.  The  specified addresses are edited by\n523:               typing in new instructions. Typing one or more spaces leaves the\n524:               core  address  unchanged, just hitting <return> repeats the last\n525:               input, and a syntax error aborts the edit. The full Redcode syn-\n526:               tax including labels and (multi-line) EQUates can be used. Label\n527:               and EQUate definitions remain in effect until the program termi-\n528:               nates.   The  edit  command is useful for modifying warriors and\n529:               trying out  single  instructions  without  having  to  exit  and\n530:               restart pMARS.\n531: \n532:        fill [range]\n533:               is  similar  to  edit.   Instructions in the specified range are\n534:               replaced by one typed in instruction. Entering DAT.F  0,0  ,e.g.\n535:               clears the address range.\n536: \n537:        search [pattern]\n538:               searches  core  instructions  for  a text pattern in the forward\n539:               direction. The next instruction matching [pattern] is displayed.\n540:               The  search includes the address number and trace symbol (T), is\n541:               case- and space-insensitive and may contain wildcards: * (aster-\n542:               iks) matches any number of characters; ? (question mark) matches\n543:               exactly one character. E.g. \"search ,\"  searches  for  the  next\n544:               non-blank  address; \"search dat*, ?0t\" searches for the next DAT\n545:               instruction that is traced  and  has  a  zero  B-operand  value,\n546:               regardless of modifier, A-operand and B-mode.\n547: \n548:        write [file]\n549:               opens  a  file for logging subsequent cdb output to. The logfile\n550:               is closed by issuing write without an argument.\n551: \n552:        echo [string]\n553:               is used mostly inside macros. [string] is echoed to  the  screen\n554:               followed by <newline>.\n555: \n556:        remark [string]\n557:               is ignored by cdb and can therefore be used to comment macros.\n558: \n559:        cls    clears  the  screen.  The  no-display  UNIX version does this by\n560:               echoing an ANSI escape sequence; if this doesn't work  for  you,\n561:               you  need to change the CLRSCR string in config.h and recompile.\n562:               clear is a synonym for cls .\n563: \n564:        display clear|on|off|nnn\n565:               (available in display versions only) allows  clearing  the  core\n566:               display  (display  clear) or changing the display mode.  display\n567:               on changes the display to the default mode, display off (same as\n568:               display  0  )  suspends  all  display updates, and display nnn ,\n569:               where nnn is a 1 to 3-digit number, sets  the  display  to  this\n570:               mode.  \"nnn\" is interpreted like the parameter to the -v command\n571:               line option (see APPENDIX).\n572: \n573:        switch [1|2]\n574:               (available in display versions only) makes the left (1) or right\n575:               (2)  panel  the  current  panel for cdb output. Without a number\n576:               argument switch changes to the other panel. If the  right  panel\n577:               doesn't exist (initially, or after close, see below), it is cre-\n578:               ated first.\n579: \n580:        close  (available in display versions only) closes the right cdb  panel\n581:               (if it exists) and makes the left panel fullscreen.\n582: \n583:        calc expr1[,expr2]\n584:               is  a  command  line  calculator. Since calc has no side-effects\n585:               other than echoing the result of expression 1 (and expression  2\n586:               if  provided).  In  the context of cdb macros it is also used to\n587:               assign values to the register variables 'c' through 'z'.\n588: \n589:        macro [name][,file]\n590:               loads, executes or lists macros. A macro expands to one line  of\n591:               cdb  commands  separated by the tilde character (~) (a so-called\n592:               command chain, see below).  The command macro name executes  the\n593:               macro  \"name\";  if  \"name\"  is left out, all currently available\n594:               macros are listed.  macro name,file loads macro definitions from\n595:               file \"file\" and executes macro \"name\"; again, if \"name\" is miss-\n596:               ing, only a listing is produced. Macro definitions are  appended\n597:               to the list of previously loaded definitions or replace a previ-\n598:               ously loaded macro definition with the same  name.  If  you  are\n599:               trying to execute or list macros, but no macros have been loaded\n600:               yet, the default macro file \"pmars.mac\" is loaded automatically.\n601:               The  special  macro  file \"user\" can be specified to input macro\n602:               definitions directly from the keyboard. Macro  definitions  con-\n603:               sist  of a macro name, followed by the equal sign, followed by a\n604:               command (chain).  The macro name can consist  of  any  printable\n605:               character  excluding  <space>  and comma; the equal sign is only\n606:               allowed at the end of a macro name.  Individual macro lines have\n607:               a  limit  of  80 characters, but macro calls inside macro expan-\n608:               sions are allowed.  Cdb can hold up to  200  macros  in  memory.\n609:               See also the section on cdb macro programming below.\n610: \n611:        if <expression>\n612:               controls  execution  of commands in macros or command chains. If\n613:               <expression> evaluates  to  zero,  the  next  command  block  is\n614:               skipped.  A command block consists of either a single command or\n615:               any number of commands bracketed by !!  (loop  start)  and  ![e]\n616:               (loop  end,  see  section on macro programming below).  <expres-\n617:               sion> may contain C-style comparison and boolean operators  (see\n618:               below).  An if immediately preceeding a loop end (![e]) can skip\n619:               out of the loop.\n620: \n621:        reset  is used inside macros in conjunction with if to terminate  macro\n622:               execution,    e.g.    inside    an    infinite    loop   (...~if\n623:               A==0~reset~...~!).\n624: \n625:        pqueue [1|2|..|off]\n626:               switches cdb into \"process queue mode\". In this mode, list, edit\n627:               and fill operate on the process queue instead of the core array,\n628:               i.e. you can view and modify the process queue as easily as  the\n629:               core  array. This is especially useful for debugging complicated\n630:               multi-process  warriors.   pqueue  without  argument  uses   the\n631:               process queue of the current warrior. With argument 1,2,.., uses\n632:               the process queue of warrior 1,2,.., respectively.   pqueue  off\n633:               returns to normal mode.\n634: \n635:        wqueue [off]\n636:               stands for \"warrior queue\" and is similar to pqueue, except that\n637:               numbers provided as arguments for list, edit and fill now  refer\n638:               to  warriors:  \"list 0\" now shows the program counter of warrior\n639:               1, \"list 1\" that of warrior 2 and so on.  wqueue off returns  to\n640:               normal \"address mode\".\n641: \n642:        pspace [1|2|..|off]\n643:               complements the pqueue and wqueue commands. If a number is spec-\n644:               ified, the P-space of that warrior is selected for viewing/edit-\n645:               ing. Without an argument, the P-space of the currently executing\n646:               warrior is selected. \"pspace off\" returns to core mode.\n647: \n648:        go, step, continue and thread may have a single address  argument.  The\n649:        program  counter  of  the current warrior is set to this address before\n650:        execution continues.\n651: \n652:        The range argument of the list, trace, etc.  commands  has  the  format\n653:        <start>,<stop>.  Addresses <start> and <stop> are numbers, special sym-\n654:        bols or C-style  expressions  including  special  symbols.   If  either\n655:        <start>  or  <stop> is omitted, it defaults to the current address.  If\n656:        both are omitted, the range of the last cdb command is used.  A  single\n657:        address (without the comma) acts on only that address. Addresses start-\n658:        ing with a + or - are interpreted relative to the current address.\n659: \n660:        Expressions may contain the arithmetic  operators  -,+,*,/,%  (modulo),\n661:        the  comparison  operators ==, !=, <=, >=, and the boolean operators &&\n662:        (AND), || (OR), and ! (negation).  Expressions may also include  regis-\n663:        ter  variables  C  through  Z  and  the assignment operator =. Operator\n664:        precedence is like that of the C-language  and  may  be  overridden  by\n665:        parentheses.  Assignment,  comparison and boolean operations are mostly\n666:        used with calc and if commands in macros, but can also be used in  Red-\n667:        code operands.\n668: \n669:        Special address symbols used in cdb commands:\n670: \n671:         .     (dot) is the current address (displayed last).\n672:         $     (dollar) is the last core address.\n673:         A     is the A value of the current instruction.\n674:         B     is the B value of the current instruction.\n675:         PC    is the program counter of the currently executing warrior.\n676:         PC1   is the program counter of warrior 1.\n677:         PC2   is the program counter of warrior 2.\n678:         LINES is the number of lines available to the cdb display\n679:         CYCLE is the current execution cycle (counted down)\n680: \n681:        In  process  queue  (pq),  warrior  queue (wq) or pspace (ps) mode (see\n682:        pqueue, wqueue, pspace), most of these symbols have a  different  mean-\n683:        ing:\n684: \n685:         .     (dot) is the current process number (pq),\n686:               warrior (wq), or P-space cell (ps) which was displayed last.\n687:         $     (dollar) is the last process in the process queue (pq),\n688:               the last warrior (wq), or the last P-space cell (ps).\n689:         A     is the A value of the instruction of the current process (pq),\n690:               the next executing process of the current warrior (wq), or\n691:               the P-space selector (ps, same as warrior number if unshared).\n692:         B     is the B value of the instruction of the current process (pq),\n693:               the next executing process of the current warrior (wq), or\n694:               the P-space selector (ps).\n695:         PC    is 0.\n696:         PC1.. are 0\n697: \n698:        Preceding  a  command with the character '@' (ampersand)  will suppress\n699:        its screen output, but not output to a logfile.   Preceding  a  command\n700:        with  '&' will suppress both screen and logfile output, which is useful\n701:        if you are only interested in the \"side-effects\" of a command.   Start-\n702:        ing  a  command  with  a  <Space> character suppresses saving it to the\n703:        \"last-command\" buffer that is recalled by <Enter>.\n704: \n705: COMMAND CHAINS AND MACRO PROGRAMMING\n706:        Several commands can be issued on one line when separated by the  tilde\n707:        character  (~).  These  \"command  chains\" are useful for repeating long\n708:        command sequences, since <Enter> recalls  the  entire  chain  (see  the\n709:        examples  below).   Commands  requiring user intervaention (list, edit,\n710:        fill) also read their input from the chain.\n711: \n712:        The \"empty command\" (two consecutive tildes or a tilde at  the  end  of\n713:        the chain) repeats the last command in the chain.  A command consisting\n714:        of <Space> is a null command and is used to simulate  pressing  <Enter>\n715:        in list, edit and fill.\n716: \n717:        The  exclamation mark (!) character is a special \"chain repetitor\" com-\n718:        mand. The optional expression following '!' specifies  how  many  times\n719:        the command chain starting at the beginning of the line or the last '!'\n720:        is executed. '!' without an expression repeats until the program termi-\n721:        nates.\n722: \n723:        The  symbol '!!' is used for nested loops and marks the start of a com-\n724:        mand block to be repeated. The command block is  closed  by  '![expres-\n725:        sion]'  and  may  contain other command blocks. A command block immedi-\n726:        ately following an if command is executed  only  if  the  condition  is\n727:        true.\n728: \n729:        With  loops,  subroutines  (macros  calling  macros), variables (C..Z),\n730:        expressions involving comparisons and boolean  operations,  and  condi-\n731:        tional  execution  (if),  the  cdb command language can be used to con-\n732:        struct complicated macros for e.g. executing a warrior until a  certain\n733:        core  address  has  changed, controlling the 2-panel display, automati-\n734:        cally finding the right constants for a  warrior,  etc.  See  the  file\n735:        \"pmars.mac\" for examples.\n736: \n737: EXAMPLE CDB COMMANDS\n738:        list ,+20\n739:               lists the next 20 instructions.\n740: \n741:        trace pc-10,pc+10\n742:               traces  21  addresses centered around the program counter of the\n743:               currently executing warrior.\n744: \n745:        untrace 0,$\n746:               clears all trace bits.\n747: \n748:        go   reg   l+a,+b\n749:               chains these commands: execute until the next traced address  or\n750:               end of round, display the simulator status and list addresses in\n751:               the range A-number to B-number of the current instruction.\n752: \n753:        @fill0,100 dat.f 0,0\n754:               fills addresses 0 through 100 with 'dat.f 0,0', not echoing  the\n755:               changed addresses to the screen.\n756: \n757:        write trace.log step !\n758:               produces  a  continuous  execution trace by repeating step until\n759:               pMARS terminates, saving the output to logfile \"trace.log\".\n760: \n761:        @l x=5 !! @ed x~dat x,0 if (x=x+1)<$+1 !\n762:               This command chain could be useful for debugging  a  stone-type,\n763:               self-modifying  warrior,  which  is  assumed to occupy address 0\n764:               through 4 in this example. The command fills  core  starting  at\n765:               address  5  with  \"dat  5,0\", \"dat 6,0\", a.s.o., so that you can\n766:               tell where a bomb which overwrites the  warrior  came  from.  To\n767:               save some typing, you can turn this command into a macro (foo=@l\n768:               x=5~..). This is how it works, step by step: Assign 5 to  regis-\n769:               ter  x  and  make  it the current address (@l x=5). Start a loop\n770:               (!!) and change address x to \"dat x,0\" (@ed x~dat  x,0).  Incre-\n771:               ment  x, if x is then smaller than the core size ($+1), continue\n772:               looping (if (x=x+1)<$+1~!). The '@' in front  of  the  list  and\n773:               edit commands suppresses screen output.\n774: \n775:        @s @4 if b<2 || b>=$-3 reset !\n776:               This  command  executes a warrior until the B-field of address 4\n777:               points to address 0 through 5: Step and make address 4 the  cur-\n778:               rent  address  (@s~@4). If the B-field is less than 2 or greater\n779:               than or equal to 7996 (CORESIZE-1-3) stop execution,  else  con-\n780:               tinue looping (if b<2 || b>=$-3~reset~!).\n781: \n782: SOURCE DEBUGGING DIRECTIVES\n783:        Trace  bits can also be set by including debugging commands in the war-\n784:        rior source. A comment format is used to retain compatibility with sim-\n785:        ulators that do not support source-embedded debugging commands.\n786: \n787:        ;debug [static/off]\n788:               This  command  enables/disables  all  subsequent source-embedded\n789:               commands.  It is used for commenting out other source  comments.\n790:               ;debug static has the same effect as the command moveable off at\n791:               the cdb command prompt.  ;debug is implicitly added in front  of\n792:               every  warrior.  The  last  ;debug  or ;debug static encountered\n793:               specifies whether the trace bit is copied by a MOV.I instruction\n794:               or not.\n795: \n796:        ;trace [off]\n797:               ;trace  starts  setting  the trace bit with the next instruction\n798:               until EOF or a ;trace off command is encountered.\n799: \n800:        ;break sets the trace bit of the next instruction.\n801: \n802: BUGS\n803:        None whatsoever (right).  Contact for bug reports  and  suggestions  is\n804:        Stefan  Strack  (stst@vuse.vanderbilt.edu).   Please  be  detailed  and\n805:        include a logfile of the cdb session if  applicable. In text mode,  a  black  '0'  on\n851:               blue background is shown for warrior 1, a black '1' on green for\n852:               warrior 2, a.s.o.. These colors are also  used\n855:               for other core accesses.\n856: \n857:        2      Also  display write accesses. In text mode, they appear as dots;\n858:               in graphics mode, they appear as two pixels, offset diagonally.\n859: \n860:        3      Also display decrements and increments. They are  shown  as  '+'\n861:               and '-' in text mode and as two pixels offset vertically or hor-\n862:               izontally in graphics mode.\n863: \n864:        4      Also display read accesses, which appear as small dots  in  text\n865:               mode and as single pixels in graphics mode.\n866: \n867:        The  more  is  displayed, the slower runs the simulation.  The argument\n868:        for -v defaults to 103, i.e. speed=1, mode=text, level=3.\n869: \n870:        The text mode display is very fast, but contains less on-screen  infor-\n871:        mation than the graphics display. The core display and the cdb debugger\n872:        run full-screen on separate display pages.\n873: \n874:        In graphics mode, core and debugger share the same  screen.  The  mouse\n875:        can be used to navigate around core when debugging is enabled: clicking\n876:        a mouse button on any core location lists addresses starting there. The\n877:        mouse  cursor  follows  the current program counter when in single step\n878:        mode.\n879: \n880:        In both graphics and text mode, the cdb display can be divided into two\n881:        side-by-side panels. You can switch between panels with the switch com-\n882:        mand (or the <Tab> macro) and close the right panel with close (or  the\n883:        <Shft-Tab> macro).  Extended (function keys, arrow/page keys, ALT keys,\n884:        etc.) and control keys generate macro calls at the cdb prompt; some  of\n885:        these \"hot key macros\" have been defined in \"pmars.mac\"; you can easily\n886:        change them or add more with a text editor.   E.g.  <PgDn>  and  <PgUp>\n887:        keys  currently  invoke macros that scroll through core one screen at a\n888:        time.\n889: \n890:        A white line at the top of the display, called the  time  meter,  indi-\n891:        cates the time required to finish the current simulation. The amount of\n892:        time depends on the number of warriors still alive in the arena.  After\n893:        a  warrior dies it no longer needs simulation time so the required time\n894:        to finish the simulation becomes less. On the time meter this is  indi-\n895:        cated  by a discontinuity. One can count the number of dead warriors in\n896:        the arena by counting the number of discontinuities on the time meter.\n897: \n898:        Just below, the length of \"process meters\" in the color of the warriors\n899:        they represent show how many processes each warrior has running.\n900: \n901:        The following keys are available at the core display screen:\n902: \n903:        0..4   selects the display level (see above).\n904: \n905:        v      switches from text display to graphics display and vice versa.\n906: \n907:        >      increases the display speed.\n908: \n909:        <      decreases the display speed. E.g.:\n923:        key-p= progress~registers~continue\n924:        Function-key and other macros can also be invoked from  the  core  dis-\n925:        play.\n926: \n927: CURSES DISPLAY\n928:        The  curses display is very similar to the DOS text mode display.
